plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic drawing of a polarimeter, laid out as a single optical path running left to right in perspective. At the far left a lit incandescent bulb sits in a socket inside a yellow glow, labeled "Light source", and short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions emerge from it beneath the label "Unpolarized light". The beam is drawn as a flat pale yellow ribbon that passes through a circular disc with fine vertical striping, labeled "Polarizer", after which the red arrows all lie in a single vertical plane under the label "Polarized light". The ribbon then runs through a horizontal cylinder with a small filling stub on top, drawn with rounded ends and labeled "Sample tube containing organic molecules"; the red arrows inside progressively tip away from vertical as they move along the tube. Beyond the tube the beam meets a second striped disc labeled "Analyzer" and continues to the right, where a heavy red double-headed arrow lies at a slant. A vertical dashed reference line and a curved arrow mark the angle between the two, labeled with the Greek letter alpha, and a drawn eye at the right edge is labeled "Observer". Tracking one ribbon of light through every component makes the tilt of the arrows the quantity to follow. The arrangement shows how the rotation an optically active sample imposes on the plane of polarization is measured.

interactions.label: Analyzer rotation
interactions.teaches: Rotating the analyzer disc lets the observer hunt for maximum brightness; the angle read off the arc equals the sample's optical rotation when the transmitted beam is brightest

interactions.label: Sample optical rotation α
interactions.teaches: An optically active sample twists the plane of polarization by an amount set by the sample — the arrows inside the tube wind progressively and the emergent beam leaves at the tilted angle the analyzer must match

interactions.label: Send light pulse
interactions.teaches: Watching one pulse travel the path clarifies each component's role: unpolarized light enters, the polarizer passes one plane, the sample rotates that plane, and the analyzer passes or blocks it depending on its angle

demo_steps.title: Achiral sample
demo_steps.narration: With optical rotation zero, the arrows stay vertical through the tube and the beam emerges upright — the analyzer reads maximum brightness at 0°, matching the polarizer.

demo_steps.title: Optically active sample
demo_steps.narration: Increase the sample rotation to +30°. The arrows inside the tube twist progressively and the emergent arrow tilts; the fixed analyzer now dims the beam because its stripes no longer align with the plane.

demo_steps.title: Find α with the analyzer
demo_steps.narration: Rotate the analyzer to +30° until transmission is maximal. The curved arc from the vertical dashed line to the analyzer orientation is the measured rotation α reported for the sample.

demo_steps.title: Levorotatory sample
demo_steps.narration: Set the rotation negative (−30°): the arrows twist the opposite way, and the analyzer must be turned to −30° — the sign of α distinguishes the two enantiomers.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Optical path runs left→right along world +X, beam height Y≈0, depth ±1.5. Bulb at x≈-5: small sphere (~0.5 r) with glow sprite, warm yellow #fff2a8; socket base grey disc. Unpolarized arrows: 6 red (#d21f26) double-headed arrows in a fan at x≈-4.3, radiating in the transverse plane. Beam: flat pale-yellow (#ffe9a0, opacity ~0.5) ribbon ~0.35 tall, running x=-5 to +6.5. Polarizer disc at x≈-3: radius ~1.1, thin cylinder perpendicular to X, tan rim with vertical stripe texture. Sample tube x from -2.4 to +1.6: horizontal translucent cylinder radius ~0.85, pale green-grey glass (#c8d6c4, opacity 0.35) with rounded end caps and a small stub cylinder on top near x≈0.6. Inside tube: 5-6 red double-headed arrows along X in the vertical transverse plane, each rotated about the X-axis by an angle interpolating 0→α across the tube length. Analyzer disc at x≈+3.2, radius ~1.05, same style as polarizer but stripes rotated by analyzerAngle about X. Outgoing arrow: heavy red double-headed arrow at x≈+4.3 tilted by the emergent angle. At x≈+4.8: vertical dashed reference line, curved arc with arrowhead from the vertical to the outgoing arrow direction, labeled α in italics. Eye icon at x≈+6.2. Perspective is mild, viewed slightly from front-above as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Stripe textures on both discs can be canvas-generated concentric line patterns; rotate analyzer texture with analyzerAngle. Transmitted brightness: modulate outgoing beam/arrow opacity and a small glow at the eye by cos²(analyzerAngle − α) (Malus's law) so 'finding α' is visible. Tube interior arrows interpolate their X-axis rotation linearly with position for the progressive twist; animate this smoothly as opticalActivity changes. Pulse animation: a bright blob travels left→right; pre-polarizer it shows a spinning multi-direction arrow, post-polarizer a single vertical arrow, in-tube the arrow twists, and at the analyzer it is passed (bright) or blocked (fades) per Malus's law. Labels as sprites/CSS2D always facing camera.

authoredContext:
The angle of rotation can be measured with an instrument called a polarimeter, represented in the figure. A solution of optically active organic molecules is placed in a sample tube, plane-polarized light is passed through the tube, and rotation of the polarization plane occurs. The light then goes through a second polarizer called the analyzer. By rotating the analyzer until the light passes through it, we can find the new plane of polarization and can tell to what extent rotation has occurred.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Plane-polarized light passes through a solution of optically active molecules, which rotate the plane of polarization.

Schematic representation of a polarimeter. Unpolarized light from light source passes through polarizer, followed by polarized light, sample tube containing organic molecules, analyzer, and observer.

In addition to determining the extent of rotation, we can also find the direction. From the vantage point of the observer looking directly at the analyzer, some optically active molecules rotate polarized light to the left (counterclockwise) and are said to be levorotatory, whereas others rotate polarized light to the right (clockwise) and are said to be dextrorotatory. By convention, rotation to the left is given a minus sign (−) and rotation to the right is given a plus sign (+). (−)-Morphine, for example, is levorotatory, and (+)-sucrose is dextrorotatory.

plan.contextChunk: This figure is a schematic drawing of a polarimeter, laid out as a single optical path running left to right in perspective. At the far left a lit incandescent bulb sits in a socket inside a yellow glow, labeled "Light source", and short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions emerge from it beneath the label "Unpolarized light". The beam is drawn as a flat pale yellow ribbon that passes through a circular disc with fine vertical striping, labeled "Polarizer", after which the red arrows all lie in a single vertical plane under the label "Polarized light". The ribbon then runs through a horizontal cylinder with a small filling stub on top, drawn with rounded ends and labeled "Sample tube containing organic molecules"; the red arrows inside progressively tip away from vertical as they move along the tube. Beyond the tube the beam meets a second striped disc labeled "Analyzer" and continues to the right, where a heavy red double-headed arrow lies at a slant. A vertical dashed reference line and a curved arrow mark the angle between the two, labeled with the Greek letter alpha, and a drawn eye at the right edge is labeled "Observer". Tracking one ribbon of light through every component makes the tilt of the arrows the quantity to follow. The arrangement shows how the rotation an optically active sample imposes on the plane of polarization is measured.

elements: incandescent light bulb in a socket base at far left, with yellow glow
unpolarized light: fan of short red double-headed arrows pointing in many directions just right of the bulb
pale yellow ribbon beam running left-to-right through the entire apparatus
polarizer disc with fine vertical stripes, standing perpendicular to the beam
sample tube: horizontal translucent cylinder with rounded ends and a small filling stub on top
series of red double-headed polarization arrows inside the tube, progressively tipped away from vertical along its length
analyzer disc with fine stripes, standing perpendicular to the beam right of the tube
outgoing red double-headed arrow to the right of the analyzer, lying at a slant
vertical dashed reference line near the observer
curved arrow arc marking angle alpha between the vertical reference and the outgoing arrow, labeled α
drawn eye at the right edge labeled Observer
labels: Light source, Unpolarized light, Polarizer, Polarized light, Sample tube containing organic molecules, Analyzer, α, Observer

interactions.label: Analyzer rotation
interactions.teaches: Rotating the analyzer disc lets the observer hunt for maximum brightness; the angle read off the arc equals the sample's optical rotation when the transmitted beam is brightest

interactions.label: Sample optical rotation α
interactions.teaches: An optically active sample twists the plane of polarization by an amount set by the sample — the arrows inside the tube wind progressively and the emergent beam leaves at the tilted angle the analyzer must match

interactions.label: Send light pulse
interactions.teaches: Watching one pulse travel the path clarifies each component's role: unpolarized light enters, the polarizer passes one plane, the sample rotates that plane, and the analyzer passes or blocks it depending on its angle

demo_steps.title: Achiral sample
demo_steps.narration: With optical rotation zero, the arrows stay vertical through the tube and the beam emerges upright — the analyzer reads maximum brightness at 0°, matching the polarizer.

demo_steps.title: Optically active sample
demo_steps.narration: Increase the sample rotation to +30°. The arrows inside the tube twist progressively and the emergent arrow tilts; the fixed analyzer now dims the beam because its stripes no longer align with the plane.

demo_steps.title: Find α with the analyzer
demo_steps.narration: Rotate the analyzer to +30° until transmission is maximal. The curved arc from the vertical dashed line to the analyzer orientation is the measured rotation α reported for the sample.

demo_steps.title: Levorotatory sample
demo_steps.narration: Set the rotation negative (−30°): the arrows twist the opposite way, and the analyzer must be turned to −30° — the sign of α distinguishes the two enantiomers.

interactionPlan.geometry_notes: Optical path runs left→right along world +X, beam height Y≈0, depth ±1.5. Bulb at x≈-5: small sphere (~0.5 r) with glow sprite, warm yellow #fff2a8; socket base grey disc. Unpolarized arrows: 6 red (#d21f26) double-headed arrows in a fan at x≈-4.3, radiating in the transverse plane. Beam: flat pale-yellow (#ffe9a0, opacity ~0.5) ribbon ~0.35 tall, running x=-5 to +6.5. Polarizer disc at x≈-3: radius ~1.1, thin cylinder perpendicular to X, tan rim with vertical stripe texture. Sample tube x from -2.4 to +1.6: horizontal translucent cylinder radius ~0.85, pale green-grey glass (#c8d6c4, opacity 0.35) with rounded end caps and a small stub cylinder on top near x≈0.6. Inside tube: 5-6 red double-headed arrows along X in the vertical transverse plane, each rotated about the X-axis by an angle interpolating 0→α across the tube length. Analyzer disc at x≈+3.2, radius ~1.05, same style as polarizer but stripes rotated by analyzerAngle about X. Outgoing arrow: heavy red double-headed arrow at x≈+4.3 tilted by the emergent angle. At x≈+4.8: vertical dashed reference line, curved arc with arrowhead from the vertical to the outgoing arrow direction, labeled α in italics. Eye icon at x≈+6.2. Perspective is mild, viewed slightly from front-above as in the source.
interactionPlan.notes: Stripe textures on both discs can be canvas-generated concentric line patterns; rotate analyzer texture with analyzerAngle. Transmitted brightness: modulate outgoing beam/arrow opacity and a small glow at the eye by cos²(analyzerAngle − α) (Malus's law) so 'finding α' is visible. Tube interior arrows interpolate their X-axis rotation linearly with position for the progressive twist; animate this smoothly as opticalActivity changes. Pulse animation: a bright blob travels left→right; pre-polarizer it shows a spinning multi-direction arrow, post-polarizer a single vertical arrow, in-tube the arrow twists, and at the analyzer it is passed (bright) or blocked (fades) per Malus's law. Labels as sprites/CSS2D always facing camera.
